paper_title: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create a human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against a TF-IDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations Amirreza MOHSENI a, Gerasimos SPANAKIS Maastricht University, Maastricht, The Netherlands Abstract. People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against TFIDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development. Keywords. legal natural language processing, conversational AI, legal guidance seeking 1. Introduction People use conversational AI to seek both legal information and advice about what action to take [1]. In our dataset, these questions span topics such as Immigration & Citizenship, Employment & Labor, Housing & Property, Business & Commercial, and Consumer & Personal Finance. Prominent legal NLP benchmarks evaluate legaldocument understanding, retrieval, answer generation, or expert-defined reasoning tasks [2,3,4,5]. They reveal less about the more basic question faced by general-purpose assistant: when is person actually seeking legal guidance, and how are such requests formulated in the wild? Legally themed text is not synonymous with guidance seeking. user may ask for statute to be translated, discuss fictional dispute, request an academic explanation, or describe personal situation while seeking concrete rights, options, or next steps. We therefore study hierarchical classification problem over real LLM conversations: the Accepted for publication at JURIX 2026, Toulouse, France. first stage predicts whether the user seeks personalized or practical legal guidance, and the second assigns each positive conversation to one of 14 primary legal topics. The distinction matters because public-facing LLMs can confidently produce unreliable legal information [6]: compact guidance detector could support large-scale extraction for empirical research or, after calibration and user testing, trigger notice that generated output is not substitute for professional advice. This framing parallels recent work on how users seek health information from conversational systems [7]. We make four contributions. First, we develop taxonomy for identifying and characterizing requests for legal guidance in multi-turn conversations. Second, we apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations spanning both guidance-seeking and non-guidance cases and analyze how requests are formulated, when they first arise, and which legal domains they concern. Third, we release human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations and supporting artifacts.1 Fourth, we compare lexical cascade with ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large [8], evaluating them on the gold evaluation set only after finalizing all modeling decisions using separate silver-labeled development data. 2. Related Work Legal information needs. Prior work has examined both observed requests to legal-help AI and users expectations of such systems. Kuk and Haraˇsta study queries submitted to GPT-4 legal assistant and distinguish requests for legal information from requests for advice about what action to take [1]. Hagan uses interviews and design sessions to examine when people would use legal-help AI and which qualities and safeguards they expect from it [9]. Steenhuis and Westermann use LLMs to support civil legal-aid intake by checking eligibility and generating follow-up questions [10]. We study an upstream and broader task in naturally occurring conversations: identifying whether users seek legal guidance and how they formulate those requests. Behavior in real-world conversations. WildChat makes it possible to study interactions with conversational models at scale [11]. close methodological analogue is Whats Up, Doc?, which filters large conversational datasets and applies clinician-driven taxonomy to how and why users seek health information across specialties [7]. We adopt the same user-centered perspective for law, but separate legal content from guidance seeking and add hierarchical topic classification, supporting both descriptive analysis and smaller classifiers that apply the taxonomy without repeatedly invoking frontier model. Legal NLP. Prominent benchmarks evaluate legal-document understanding or expertdefined reasoning tasks [2,3]. complementary line of work starts from citizen or lay legal questions. BSARD maps French questions to relevant Belgian statutory provisions, and Finding the Law studies improved statutory retrieval in the same citizen-question setting [4,12]. LLeQA pairs expert-annotated questions with long-form answers grounded in legislation [5], while GerLayQA pairs German civil-law questions from laypeople with lawyer-authored answers and statutory references [13]. These resources provide useful evidence about question language, legal-topic distributions, retrieval, and answer generation in fixed-question settings. We instead examine the distributions of guidance 1https://github.com/Amir-Mohseni/Legal-Guidance-in-the-Wild intent, request types, and legal topics in naturally occurring, multi-turn conversations. Topic taxonomies provide useful structure for legal datasets [14], but assigning an interaction directly to legal field misses whether the user wants explanation, drafting, procedural steps, or advice about rights and options. Strong benchmark performance also does not make public model reliable legal adviser: Dahl et al. document frequent legal hallucinations and confident acceptance of false premises [6]. Our classifier does not assess answer correctness; it identifies conversations in which stronger safeguards, specialized routing, or human escalation may be warranted. 3. Data and Task 3.1. Dataset construction, taxonomy, and silver annotation The conversations originate from English-language WildChat-1M interaction logs [11]. We used OpenAIs GPT-5.6 Terra, accessed through the OpenAI API at high reasoning effort, for an initial screening pass to identify clearly unrelated material and conversations potentially containing legal content [15]. The retained sample contains 2,122 conversations, combining conversations initially identified as containing legal content with an equal-sized random sample from those classified by Terra as non-legal. These initial labels determined sample composition and are distinct from the annotations used in our analysis. This design allows building classification models; however, the label distribution cannot estimate prevalence in WildChat. The taxonomy captures three aspects of conversation. Its legal relevance axis distinguishes legal content from personalized or practical guidance seeking. Its interaction axis records user context, drafting intent, guidance onset, and request types: rights-andoptions advice, information or explanation, procedural assistance, document drafting, document review, and other requests. Its domain axis assigns legal topics. We adapted the topic and subtopic structure of existing literature [4,12]. The domain axis concerns 13 substantive legal topics and residual OTHER category. Each conversation receives one primary topic representing its predominant legal issue and optional secondary topics for additional issues. The domain axis is flat; the classification pipeline first detects guidance seeking and then predicts primary topic. The other taxonomy fields support descriptive analysis. Following screening and sample selection, we annotated all 2,122 retained conversations with OpenAIs GPT-5.6 Sol, accessed through the OpenAI API at medium reasoning effort under the taxonomy [15]. Sol annotated every retained conversation, including the non-guidance cases; Terras screening labels were not used as the final silver labels. These Sol annotations form the silver-labeled dataset: 1,367 conversations contain legal content and 972 seek legal guidance (45.8%). All classifiers and descriptive analyses use these annotations, with human-reviewed labels replacing them for gold evaluation. Only user messages are presented, in chronological order; assistant messages are excluded because we study how users phrase legal requests. The dataset, annotation prompt, JSON schema, and run configurations are available through the project resources. 2 We retain fixed 200-conversation subset for human review. It was sampled using the initial guidance labels to include 100 guidance-positive and 100 guidance-negative 2https://huggingface.co/collections/AmirMohseni/legal-guidance-in-the-wild Split Guidance Legal content Human guidance Silver-labeled dataset Silver development set Train Validation Gold evaluation set 2,122 1,922 1,632 290 200 972 (45.8%) 884 (46.0%) 750 (46.0%) 134 (46.2%) 88 (44.0%) 1,367 (64.4%) 1,232 (64.1%) 1,048 (64.2%) 184 (63.4%) 135 (67.5%) 84 (42.0%) Table 1. Dataset and label summary. The Guidance and Legal content columns report silver labels; the last column reports the final human-reviewed guidance labels, which exist only for the gold evaluation set and replace the corresponding silver guidance labels during evaluation. The dataset was enriched during screening, so these percentages are not WildChat prevalence estimates. conversations; topic was not used for selection. After Sol annotation and human review, this gold evaluation set contains 84 guidance-positive and 116 guidance-negative conversations. The other 1,922 conversations form the silver development set, split into 1,632 training and 290 validation conversations. The split was stratified first by guidance and then, among guidance-positive conversations where counts allowed, by primary topic  (Table 1)  . The term silver-labeled dataset refers to all 2,122 Sol annotations, including those of the evaluation conversations before human review. Table 2 reports the complete primary-topic distribution. 3.2. Human review and gold evaluation set Two reviewers with backgrounds in computer science independently examined all 200 conversations in the gold evaluation set. Each reviewer worked on separate worksheet and recorded whether the silver guidance and primary-topic labels were correct, adding corrected label and short note where needed. Reviewing the silver labels rather than labeling each conversation from scratch allowed both reviewers to assess the full set, but may have introduced anchoring; we return to this in the Discussion. We measured agreement on the 200-conversation gold evaluation set using the available paired judgments. Guidance agreement was 96.5%, with Cohens κ = .927. Topic agreement, measured over binary judgments of whether the silver topic was correct, was 94.9%, with κ = .561. The lower topic κ reflects judgment imbalance: reviewers marked the silver topic as correct in 94% of judgments, and κ is sensitive to such imbalances [16]. Overall, the reviewers reached full agreement on 186 conversations (93.0%). They discussed the remaining 14 cases (7.0%) and reached consensus; these consensus decisions became the final labels. We use only the silver development set for training and model selection and reserve the gold evaluation set for final evaluation. 3.3. Task and metrics We formulate the task as two-stage classification pipeline. In Stage 1, the model identifies whether conversation contains request for legal guidance. In Stage 2, conversations identified as positive in Stage 1 are classified into one of 14 legal topics. Each conversation receives one of 15 final labels (either one of the 14 topics or NO GUIDANCE), so errors at either stage affect the final label. We report accuracy and macro-F1 for guidance detection, topic classification, and end-to-end evaluation. Macro-F1 gives equal weight to each class, which is important because several topics are rare; the supplementary material provides additional guidance metrics and confidence intervals. The primary goal of the manual annotation was to verify whether each conversation seeks legal guidance. Because guidance requests span many legal topics, the gold evaluation set provides more limited evidence for topic evaluation: its 84 guidance-positive conversations cover 12 of the 14 topics, with no examples of Torts & Civil Liability or OTHER, and five topics have five or fewer examples. We compute gold topic macro-F1 over only the 12 observed classes and provide bootstrap intervals and paired significance tests in the supplementary material. 4. How Users Seek Legal Guidance Of the 2,122 conversations in the silver-labeled dataset, 1,367 (64.4%) contain some form of legal content. Among those 1,367 conversations, 972 (71.1%) seek personalized or practical legal guidance; these guidance requests account for 45.8% of the dataset. The remaining 395 conversations discuss legal issues without seeking guidance, and 755 contain no legal content. These percentages should not be interpreted as prevalence estimates for WildChat because the sampling process deliberately included more conversations initially identified as legal. Request types. Among the 1,367 legal-content conversations, rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type (712; 52.1%), followed by information or explanation (293; 21.4%), procedural how-to (180; 13.2%), document drafting (137; 10.0%), other request (26; 1.9%), and document review (19; 1.4%). Rightsand-options advice concerns the users own situation (e.g., Can my landlord evict me for this?); information or explanation asks how legal concept or system works (e.g., What is the difference between civil and criminal law?); and procedural how-to requests ask for concrete steps, forms, or deadlines (e.g., How do file an appeal?). Document drafting asks the model to produce or revise legally operative text (e.g., Draft termination clause), whereas document review asks it to analyze an existing document (e.g., What does this clause mean?). The residual other request category covers legal-content requests outside these groups (e.g., Create quiz about contract law). Requests to create quizzes or similar study materials fall under this residual category, while requests to explain legal concepts fall under information or explanation. conversation can receive more than one request-type label. When both primary and secondary request-type labels are counted, 62.5% of conversations include rightsand-options advice and 36.6% include information or explanation. Thus, users most often ask what they can or should do in their particular situation. Explanations also appear in more than one third of conversations, often alongside request for practical guidance. Topics and guidance onset. Among the 972 guidance-seeking conversations, Immigration & Citizenship is the largest primary topic (14.1%), followed by Criminal Law (11.4%), Intellectual Property (11.3%), Business & Commercial (11.0%), and Tax Law (10.8%). The distribution has long tail: Civil Rights & Constitutional accounts for 0.3% of primary labels and Torts & Civil Liability for 1.2%. In total, 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations receive more than one topic. Secondary labels substantially increase the apparent coverage of cross-cutting domains such as Government & Administrative and Business & Commercial  (Table 2)  . Legal-topic distribution among the 972 silver-labeled guidance-positive conversations. Primary counts the predominant topic; Any also counts secondary-topic assignments and therefore does not sum to 100%. Conversations contain median of 2 user turns, and user turns contain median of 51 words. Guidance first appears after the opening user turn in 305 of 972 positives (31.4%), so 68.6% begin with guidance; these onset fields are not independently validated and are used only descriptively. The silver annotator flags medium or high uncertainty for 20.7% of conversations it labels guidance-positive, compared with 7.6% of the remaining conversations. We did not test whether these flags predict human corrections or classifier errors for this study. 5. Classification Models and Early Prediction 5.1. Experimental setup We compare two classifier families: logistic regression using wordand character-level TFIDF features, and ModernBERT encoders in base and large configurations [17,8]. We chose these models with consumer-device use in mind and aimed for an approach that could process entire datasets quickly. TFIDF with logistic regression provides lexical baseline, while ModernBERT provides contextual language-model approach. The base and large configurations allow us to examine whether increased model size consistently improves classification performance. All classifiers receive only user turns in chronological order. The training and validation splits have similar guidance rates (46.0% and 46.2%), and both contain examples from all 14 topics. Because the topic distribution is highly imbalanced, we use class-weighted topic training and macro-averaged evaluation. To support guidance detection as conversation unfolds, we also train binary prefix models. conversation prefix contains all user messages up to given turn, whereas the full-conversation models are trained only on complete conversations. Training configurations. Thresholds apply to guidance detection. Prefix thresholds maximize conversation-weighted macro-F1, using positive-class F1 as tie-breaker. and those at or after turn are labeled positive; conversations without guidance seeking contribute only negative examples. All prefixes from conversation remain within the same split, and each is weighted by the inverse of the conversations turn count, so every conversation contributes total weight of 1. This setup applies only to guidance detection; we do not train prefix topic classifier. Training configurations. Table 3 summarizes the features, optimization settings, and validation rules for the full-conversation and prefix models. The frozen prefix splits contain 4,865 training prefixes from 1,632 conversations and 912 validation prefixes from 290 conversations, including 2,042 and 376 positive prefixes, respectively. Resources. The Legal Guidance in the Wild Hugging Face collection is the consolidated entry point for the datasets, model checkpoints, training details, human-reviewed gold evaluation set, and evaluation artifacts. 5.2. Evaluation We calibrated the guidance models on the silver validation split using the thresholds in Table 3 and froze all model-selection decisions before evaluating on the gold evaluation set. The final-turn results use this locked evaluation; the exploratory turn-1 and turn-2 analysis applies the same frozen prefix checkpoints and thresholds to shorter inputs. We report 95% bootstrap intervals from 2,000 conversation-level resamples and use exact paired McNemar tests to compare system errors. Full reliability procedures and results are provided in the supplementary material. 6. Results Final-turn results come from the locked evaluation on the 200-conversation gold evaluation set. The initial-turn results come from subsequent exploratory analysis with the frozen prefix models. Full per-class topic scores are provided in the supplementary material. Model Acc. Turn 1 uses all conversations in the gold evaluation set; Turn 2 uses the 104 conversations containing at least two user turns. Labels indicate whether the complete conversation eventually seeks guidance, not whether guidance has begun by that turn. The columns use different evaluation sets and should not be interpreted as within-model improvement. 6.1. Stage 1: Guidance detection ModernBERT-large has the highest full-conversation guidance scores, with accuracy and macro-F1 both at .845  (Table 4)  . The margin over the lexical baseline is small: TFIDF reaches .840 accuracy, difference of one conversation in 200. ModernBERT-base has the lowest accuracy and macro-F1. ModernBERT-large has the highest recall, identifying 79 of 84 guidance-positive conversations (.940), compared with 75 for TFIDF and 71 for ModernBERT-base, but it also produces 26 false positives. The prefix ModernBERT-large model has the highest final-turn guidance scores, with .860 accuracy and .859 macro-F1. Table 5 provides an exploratory view of initial prefixes. From the opening turn, TFIDF has the highest macro-F1 (.826); among conversations with at least two turns, ModernBERT-large has the highest turn-2 macroF1 (.865). Because the two columns cover different conversation sets and use eventual conversation-level guidance labels, they do not measure improvement over time or correctness of guidance onset. 6.2. Topic classification Both ModernBERT models score higher than TFIDF on topic classification  (Table 6)  . Using gold guidance labels, ModernBERT-large correctly classifies 64 of 84 conversations, ModernBERT-base 63, and TFIDF 57. Their macro-F1 scores are .671, .646, and Topic only End-to-end Cascade errors Model Acc. Macro-F 95% CI Acc. Macro-F1 FP FN Topic All TFIDF + logistic regression .679 .750 ModernBERT-base .762 ModernBERT-large .559 [.441, .632] .646 [.537, .715] .671 [.538, .750] .740 .725 .755 .527 23 .544 24 .593 9 13 5 20 18 18 52 55 49 Table 6. Topic-only classification and end-to-end routing on the gold evaluation set. Topic-only evaluation uses gold guidance labels for the 84 guidance-positive conversations, which represent only 12 of the 14 classes; that fixed set is used for macro-F1 and its bootstrap intervals. End-to-end scores use all 200 conversations and the 13 classification outcomes observed in the evaluation set. Cascade errors comprise false-positive (FP) routing, false-negative (FN) routing, and wrong-topic predictions after correct positive routing (Topic). .559, respectively. In end-to-end evaluation, ModernBERT-large routes 151 of 200 conversations correctly, compared with 148 for TFIDF and 145 for ModernBERT-base. The error counts explain why the topic-only and end-to-end rankings differ. ModernBERT-base performs well on topic classification but misses 13 guidance-positive conversations at Stage 1. ModernBERT-large misses only five, giving it the best end-toend result despite producing 26 false positives. Across the three cascades, Stage-1 classification accounts for 3137 of the 4955 total errors, and false positives are the largest single error category (2326 cases). Wrong-topic predictions remain substantial (1820 cases), so improvements at either stage could change end-to-end performance. Per-class performance varies widely, particularly for topics with few gold examples. Five of the 12 observed topics have five examples or fewer, so these results are descriptive rather than stable class-level estimates. 6.3. Statistical reliability and silver-label effects No exact paired comparison reaches < .05, and the bootstrap macro-F1 intervals overlap. The clearest performance advantage of dense models over TFIDF is in topic classification, where ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large improve macro-F1 by 8.7 and 11.2 points, respectively. Model size was not predictive of performance across the tasks. The base model led the large model by 2.9 macro-F1 points on the silver validation set for topic classification, while the large model led by 2.5 points on the gold topic task. The large model also scored highest on full-conversation guidance detection and end-to-end classification. These mixed results do not show consistent advantage for either model size. 7. Discussion The results suggest that ModernBERT helps most with topic classification. Guidance requests often contain clear words and phrases associated with options, forms, deadlines, or document drafting, which may explain why TFIDF remains competitive. Topic classification requires separating related and sometimes overlapping areas of law, and both ModernBERT models perform better on this task. However, the base and large models perform differently across the silver and gold datasets, and the differences between them are not statistically significant. The errors also show practical trade-off. ModernBERT-large misses the fewest guidance requests but also incorrectly classifies the most non-guidance conversations as guidance requests. This may be acceptable for simple caution notice, but it would increase workload if flagged conversations are sent to human reviewers or specialists. The decision threshold should therefore match the intended use. Moreover, 25.3% of guidance-seeking conversations span multiple topics, while the classifier assigns just one. Consequently, some topic classification errors may stem from the presence of multiple topics, rather than incorrect predictions. Several design choices limit the scope of our findings. Training and development labels come from one language model, and reviewers assessed pre-annotated labels, which may have introduced anchoring effects [18]. Both reviewers had computer-science backgrounds, and the topic labels were not independently checked by legal expert. Request types, secondary topics, and uncertainty flags were not human-validated. The enriched sampling design supports classifier development but not prevalence estimates for WildChat. The gold evaluation set contains only 84 guidance-positive conversations across 12 observed topics, and the models were trained using single random seed. The taxonomys focus on English, its jurisdiction-agnostic design, and the reduction of multi-topic requests to one primary routing label further limit transfer to other settings. Guidance onset was not human-validated, so the initial-turn analysis measures whether eventual guidance seeking is predictable from initial turns rather than whether model detects its true onset. The conversations may describe sensitive legal circumstances despite WildChats anonymization procedures [11]. In this paper, we report aggregate results and do not reproduce conversation excerpts. The classifier identifies requests that may need safeguards or specialized treatment; it does not determine whether claim is valid or an answer is correct. Calibration, user testing, and access to human support would therefore be necessary before deployment. 8. Conclusion We introduce taxonomy and classification benchmark for studying legal guidance seeking in general-purpose LLM conversations. In this enriched sample, silver labels identify guidance seeking in 45.8% of conversations. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidancepositive conversations span multiple topic labels. On the gold evaluation set, ModernBERT-large achieves the best performance overall; however, the gains are not uniform: TFIDF performs similarly to dense models on binary guidance detection, whereas dense models lead on topic classification. No paired comparison reaches significance at this sample size, so the score differences should be interpreted cautiously. Future work should extend this taxonomy, test its robustness across languages and legal systems, and explore how classifier outputs might inform real-time caution notices or routing decisions in deployed conversational AI systems. More broadly, we hope the public release of the annotated dataset, taxonomy, and evaluation code supports both further research into legal help-seeking behavior and the development of practical safeguards in deployed systems.

sections.title: Declaration of generative AI use
sections.content: OpenAIs GPT-5.6 Terra was used during taxonomy development, and GPT-5.6 Sol was used to generate the final silver annotations, as described in Section 3. GPT-5.6 Sol was also used to refine grammar and correct LaTeX sections of the manuscript. The authors reviewed and edited the resulting content and take responsibility for the final publication.
